nodes.statement: \leanfile{M2rGroup7/SixteenClassification/Lemma3.lean} Let $G$ and $G'$ be groups, $E$ an extension type, $e : G \simeq G'$ a group isomorphism, and $R : \mathrm{RealiseExtType}~G'~E$. Then the \emph{transferred realisation} $\mathrm{transfer}(e, R)$ is the canonical realisation of $E$ by $G$ obtained by pulling $R$ back along $e$. Concretely, take $a := e^{-1}(R.a)$, $\iota := e^{-1} \circ R.\iota$, and the bijection $(x, i) \mapsto \iota(x) \cdot a^i$ as $R.\mathrm{equiv}$ composed with $e^{-1}$.
nodes.label: def:realise-transfer

nodes.statement: \leanfile{M2rGroup7/SixteenClassification/Lemma3.lean} If $G \simeq G'$ and $G'$ admits a realisation of an extension type $E$, then so does $G$.
nodes.label: lem:realise-of-mulEquiv

nodes.statement: Immediate from Definition~\ref{def:realise-transfer}.

\leanfile{M2rGroup7/SixteenClassification/Lemma3.lean} Let $G$ be a group and $H \triangleleft G$ a normal subgroup of index $2$. Then there exists $a \in G \setminus H$, and any such $a$ satisfies $a^2 \in H$ and $\mathrm{conj}_a(H) = H$. The map $h \mapsto a h a^{-1}$ is therefore an automorphism of $H$.
nodes.label: lem:inducing-element-exists

nodes.statement: Since $[G : H] = 2 > 1$, $H \neq G$, so some $a \notin H$ exists. The coset $Ha$ has order dividing $[G : H] = 2$ and is non-identity, hence order $2$. Therefore $(Ha)^2 = H$, i.e.\ $a^2 \in H$. Normality of $H$ gives $aHa^{-1} = H$ and the conjugation map $h \mapsto aha^{-1}$ restricts to an automorphism of $H$.

\leanfile{M2rGroup7/SixteenClassification/Lemma3.lean} Let $G$ be a finite group, $H \triangleleft G$ a normal subgroup of index $2$, and $a \in G \setminus H$. Set $v := a^2 \in H$ and let $\tau \in \mathrm{Aut}(H)$ be conjugation by $a$. Then the extension type $E := (H, 2, \tau, v)$ is well-defined ($\tau(v) = v$ and $\tau^2 = \mathrm{conj}_v$) and $G$ realises $E$ with inducing element $a$ and embedding $\iota : H \hookrightarrow G$.
nodes.label: lem:realise-from-normal-index-2

nodes.statement: Set $v := a^2$ and $\tau(h) := aha^{-1}$. Then $\tau(v) = a v a^{-1} = a^3 a^{-1} = a^2 = v$ and $\tau^2(h) = a^2 h a^{-2} = v h v^{-1} = \mathrm{conj}_v (h)$. The decomposition $G = H \sqcup Ha$ as cosets of $H$ gives the bijection $H \times \{0, 1\} \xrightarrow{\sim} G$, $(h, i) \mapsto h \cdot a^i$, completing the data of a realisation.

\leanfile{M2rGroup7/SixteenClassification/Lemma3.lean} Let $G$ be a group of order $16$ with a normal subgroup $H \le G$ such that $H \simeq C_8$. Then $G$ realises one of the extension types $\mathtt{ext\_16\_1}$, $\mathtt{ext\_16\_5}$, $\mathtt{ext\_16\_6}$, $\mathtt{ext\_16\_7}$, $\mathtt{ext\_16\_8}$, or $\mathtt{ext\_16\_9}$.
nodes.label: lem:realise-with-normal-C8

Then $G$ realises one of the extension types $\mathtt{ext\_16\_2}$, $\mathtt{ext\_16\_3}$, $\mathtt{ext\_16\_4}$, $\mathtt{ext\_16\_10}$, $\mathtt{ext\_16\_11}$, $\mathtt{ext\_16\_12}$, or $\mathtt{ext\_16\_13}$.
nodes.section: 5 Case analysis for normal \texorpdfstring{$K_8 = C_4 \times C_2$}{K8 = C4 x C2}
nodes.label: lem:realise-with-normal-K8

Write $H = \langle x, y angle$ with $|x| = 4$, $|y| = 2$, and $xy = yx$, so that $H = \langle x angle 	imes \langle y angle \simeq C_4 	imes C_2$. The hypothesis $|G| = 16$ together with $|H| = 8$ gives $[G : H] = 2$, so $H$ is normal of index $2$ and Lagrange yields a partition $G = H \sqcup Ha$ for any $a \in G \setminus H$. By Lemma~ef{lem:inducing-element-exists}, $G \setminus H$ is non-empty and every $b \in G \setminus H$ satisfies $b^2 \in H$, so $|b|$ is even and divides $16$. Hence $|b| \in \{2, 4, 8, 16\}$. \smallskip 
oindent \emph{Reduction to $|a| \in \{2, 4\}$.} We may assume $G$ has no element of order $8$ (and a fortiori no element of order $16$). Indeed, if some $g \in G$ has order $8$ then $\langle g angle$ is a subgroup of $G$ of index $2$, hence normal, and isomorphic to $C_8$. In that situation the theorem 	exttt{realise\_ext\_type\_if\_not\_iso\_to\_C2\_4}~(Theorem~ef{thm:realise-ext-type-if-not-iso-to-C2-4}) dispatches via Lemma~ef{lem:realise-with-normal-C8} rather than the present lemma. Choosing $a$ to be an inducing element of minimal order in $G \setminus H$ therefore gives $|a| \in \{2, 4\}$. Set $v := a^2 \in H$ and let $	au := \mathrm{conj}_a \in \mathrm{Aut}(H)$. By Lemma~ef{lem:realise-from-normal-index-2}, $G$ realises the extension type $(H, 2, 	au, v)$. \smallskip 
oindent \emph{Structure of $\mathrm{Aut}(H)$.} $\mathrm{Aut}(K_8) \simeq D_4$ has order $8$. The Lean blueprint uses three named involutions: \[ \psi_3 : (x, y) \mapsto (x^{-1}, y), \qquad \psi_5 : (x, y) \mapsto (xy, y), \qquad \psi_6 : (x, y) \mapsto (x^{-1}, x^2 y). \] A short computation shows $\psi_3$ is central in $\mathrm{Aut}(H)$ (it commutes with both $\psi_5$ and $\psi_6$), and the kernel of the natural map $\mathrm{Aut}(H) 	o \mathrm{Aut}(H[2]) \simeq S_3$ (where $H[2] = \{e, x^2, y, x^2 y\}$ is the unique Klein four-subgroup) is $\{\mathrm{id}, \psi_3, \psi_5, \psi_3 \psi_5\}$. Consequently the conjugacy classes of involutions in $\mathrm{Aut}(H)$ are \[ \{\mathrm{id}\}, \quad \{\psi_3\}, \quad \{\psi_5, \psi_3 \psi_5\}, \quad \{\psi_6, \psi_3 \psi_6\}, \] giving four conjugacy classes of order-$\le 2$ elements. The element $x^2$ is characteristic in $H$ (it is the unique square of an order-$4$ element), so it is fixed by every $\alpha \in \mathrm{Aut}(H)$; the orbit of $y$ under $\mathrm{Aut}(H)$ is $\{y, x^2 y\}$ (with $\psi_6$ interchanging them). \smallskip We split on $|a|$. \smallskip

nodes.statement: \leanfile{M2rGroup7/SixteenClassification/Classification.lean} Let $G$ be a group of order $16$ that is not isomorphic to $(C_2)^4$. Then $G$ realises one of the extension types $\mathtt{ext\_16\_1}, \dots, \mathtt{ext\_16\_13}$.
nodes.label: thm:realise-ext-type-if-not-iso-to-C2-4

nodes.statement: By the Lean lemma \texttt{exists\_normal\_C8\_or\_C4\_C2}, $G$ has either a normal subgroup isomorphic to $C_8$ or a normal subgroup isomorphic to $K_8 = C_4 \times C_2$. The two cases are handled respectively by Lemma~\ref{lem:realise-with-normal-C8} and Lemma~\ref{lem:realise-with-normal-K8}, exhausting the possibilities and yielding one of the thirteen extension types.

nodes.name: A group of order $p^2 q$ has a normal Sylow subgroup
nodes.statement: Let $p, q$ be distinct primes and let $G$ be a finite group of order $p^2 q$. Then either the number of Sylow $p$-subgroups of $G$ is $1$ (so the unique Sylow $p$-subgroup is normal) or the number of Sylow $q$-subgroups of $G$ is $1$ (so the unique Sylow $q$-subgroup is normal).
nodes.label: lem:p2q-normal-sylow

nodes.statement: Standard Sylow counting. Already established as \texttt{p2q\_group\_has\_normal\_sylow\_subgroup} in \texttt{M2rGroup7.Lemmas.SylowUtils}.

nodes.name: Sylow cardinality and index
nodes.statement: Let $p, q$ be distinct primes, $a, b \in \mathbb{N}$, and let $G$ be a finite group with $|G| = p^a q^b$. Then every Sylow $p$-subgroup of $G$ has order $p^a$ and index $q^b$.
nodes.label: lem:sylow-card-index

nodes.statement: From $|G| = p^a q^b$ and coprimality of $p^a$ and $q^b$, the multiplicity of $p$ in $|G|$ is $a$, so every Sylow $p$-subgroup has order $p^a$ by Mathlib's \texttt{Sylow.card\_eq\_multiplicity}. The index is then $|G|/p^a = q^b$ by Lagrange. Already established as \texttt{sylow\_card\_eq} and \texttt{sylow\_index\_eq}.

nodes.name: Cyclic classification of prime order
nodes.statement: If $|G| = n$ with $n$ prime, then $G \cong C_n$.
nodes.label: lem:prime-classification

nodes.statement: A group of prime order is cyclic. Two cyclic groups of equal finite order are isomorphic via Mathlib's \texttt{mulEquivOfCyclicCardEq}. Already established as \texttt{prime\_classification} in \texttt{M2rGroup7.Classification}.

nodes.name: Classification of groups of order $p^2$
nodes.statement: For any prime $p$, a group of order $p^2$ is isomorphic to either $C_{p^2}$ or $C_p \times C_p$.
nodes.label: lem:p-squared-classification

nodes.statement: Any group of order $p^2$ is abelian; either it is cyclic (and isomorphic to $C_{p^2}$) or it has exponent $p$, in which case it is a $2$-dimensional $\mathbb{F}_p$-vector space. Already established as \texttt{p\_squared\_classification}.

nodes.name: Aut$(C_{p^2}) \cong C_{p(p-1)}$
nodes.statement: For any prime $p$, $\mathrm{MulAut}(C_{p^2}) \cong C_{p(p-1)}$.
nodes.label: lem:aut-cyclic-p2

nodes.statement: $\mathrm{MulAut}(C_{p^2}) \cong (\mathbb{Z}/p^2 \mathbb{Z})^\times$, which is cyclic of order $\varphi(p^2) = p(p-1)$. Already established as \texttt{aut\_of\_cyclic\_p2}.

nodes.name: Aut$(C_p \times C_p) \cong \mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{F}_p)$
nodes.statement: For any prime $p$, $\mathrm{MulAut}(C_p \times C_p) \cong \mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{F}_p)$.
nodes.label: lem:aut-CpCp

nodes.statement: $C_p \times C_p$ is a $2$-dimensional $\mathbb{F}_p$-vector space and every additive automorphism is automatically $\mathbb{F}_p$-linear. Already established as \texttt{aut\_of\_CpCp}.

nodes.name: $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{F}_2) \cong D_3$
nodes.statement: $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{F}_2)$ is isomorphic to the dihedral group of order $6$.
nodes.label: lem:GL2F2-isoS3

nodes.statement: A direct computation: $|\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{F}_2)| = 6$ and $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{F}_2)$ is non-abelian. Already established as \texttt{GL2F2\_isoS3}.

nodes.name: Trivial homomorphism from coprime cardinalities
nodes.statement: Let $G, H$ be finite groups with $\gcd(|G|, |H|) = 1$. Then every group homomorphism $\varphi : G \to H$ satisfies $\varphi = 1$.
nodes.label: lem:eq-one-of-coprime-card

nodes.statement: The image $\varphi(G)$ is a subgroup of $H$ whose cardinality divides $\gcd(|G|,|H|) = 1$, so $|\varphi(G)| = 1$ and $\varphi$ is trivial. Already established as \texttt{eq\_one\_of\_coprime\_card}.

nodes.name: Semidirect product with trivial action is a direct product
nodes.statement: Let $N, K$ be groups and let $\varphi : K \to \mathrm{Aut}(N)$ with $\varphi = 1$. Then $N \rtimes_\varphi K \cong N \times K$.
nodes.label: lem:sdp-trivial-action

nodes.statement: The multiplication on $N \rtimes_\varphi K$, $(n_1, k_1)(n_2, k_2) = (n_1 \cdot \varphi(k_1)(n_2),\ k_1 k_2)$, reduces to $(n_1 n_2, k_1 k_2)$. Already established as \texttt{SemidirectProduct.mulEquivOfTrivialAction}.

nodes.name: Coprime cyclic direct product
nodes.statement: For positive integers $m, n$ with $\gcd(m, n) = 1$, $C_m \times C_n \cong C_{mn}$.
nodes.label: lem:cyclic-prod

nodes.statement: Already established as \texttt{CyclicGroup.prodMulEquiv}.

nodes.name: Schur--Zassenhaus complement
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be a finite group and $N \trianglelefteq G$ a normal subgroup with $\gcd(|N|, [G:N]) = 1$. Then there exists a subgroup $K \leq G$ with $N \cap K = \{1\}$ and $NK = G$.
nodes.label: lem:schur-zassenhaus

nodes.statement: Mathlib's \texttt{Subgroup.exists\_right\_complement'\_of\_coprime}.

nodes.name: Semidirect product from a complement
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be a group with $N \trianglelefteq G$ and let $K \leq G$ be a complement of $N$. Then $G \cong N \rtimes_\varphi K$ where $\varphi$ is the conjugation action of $K$ on $N$.
nodes.label: lem:sdp-from-complement

nodes.statement: Mathlib's \texttt{SemidirectProduct.mulEquivSubgroup}.

nodes.name: Transport of a semidirect product
nodes.statement: Let $f_N : N_1 \cong N_2$ and $f_K : K_1 \cong K_2$ be group isomorphisms and let $\varphi_1 : K_1 \to \mathrm{Aut}(N_1)$. Set $\varphi_2 := (\mathrm{MulAut.congr}\,f_N) \circ \varphi_1 \circ f_K^{-1}$. Then $N_1 \rtimes_{\varphi_1} K_1 \cong N_2 \rtimes_{\varphi_2} K_2$.
nodes.label: lem:sdp-congr

nodes.statement: \texttt{SemidirectProduct.congr'}; the underlying map sends $(n, k)$ to $(f_N(n), f_K(k))$.

nodes.name: Classification of semidirect products of cyclic groups
nodes.statement: Let $p, q$ be distinct primes with $q$ odd, let $m \geq 1$ and $n \geq 1$, and let $N$, $K$ be (abstract) cyclic groups with $|N| = q^n$ and $|K| = p^m$. For any homomorphism $\varphi : K \to \mathrm{Aut}(N)$ there exists a unique $r \in \{0, 1, \dots, \min(m, v_p(q-1))\}$ together with an isomorphism \[ N \rtimes_\varphi K \ \cong\ N \rtimes_{\psi_r} K, \] where $\psi_r := \mathtt{sdpCanonicalAction}(\dots, r) : K \to \mathrm{Aut}(N)$ is the canonical action of image-order $p^r$.
nodes.label: thm:classify-sdp

nodes.statement: A two-step bridge using Lemma~\ref{lem:sdp-congr}: conjugate $\varphi$ across the unique iso $N \cong C_{q^n}$ and $K \cong C_{p^m}$, apply the concrete classification on $C_{q^n} \rtimes C_{p^m}$, and conjugate back. Implemented as \texttt{classify\_sdp} in \texttt{M2rGroup7.P2qClassification.CycPGroupClassification}.

nodes.name: Range cardinality of $\psi_r$
nodes.statement: The image $\psi_r(K)$ has cardinality exactly $p^r$.
nodes.label: lem:sdp-canonical-range

nodes.statement: Already established as \texttt{sdpCanonicalAction\_range\_card}.

nodes.name: Iso of two homomorphisms with equal images
nodes.statement: Let $p$ be prime, $N$ be a finite group with $\gcd(|N|, p) = 1$, $K$ be a cyclic $p$-group with $|K| = p$, and let $f_1, f_2 : K \to \mathrm{Aut}(N)$ have the same image. Then $N \rtimes_{f_1} K \cong N \rtimes_{f_2} K$.
nodes.label: lem:sdp-iso-range-eq

nodes.statement: Already established as \texttt{semidirectProduct\_iso\_if\_range\_eq}.

nodes.name: $\varphi_1 : C_4 \to \mathrm{Aut}(C_q)$, image of order $2$
nodes.statement: For an odd prime $q$, define \[ \mathtt{canonicalC4OnCqAction} := \mathtt{sdpCanonicalAction}\bigl(\dots, m = 2,\, n = 1,\, r = 1\bigr) \,:\, C_4 \to \mathrm{Aut}(C_q). \]
nodes.label: def:canonicalC4OnCq-r1

nodes.name: $\varphi_2 : C_4 \to \mathrm{Aut}(C_q)$, image of order $4$
nodes.statement: For an odd prime $q$ with $q \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, define \[ \mathtt{canonicalC4OnCqAction\_r2} := \mathtt{sdpCanonicalAction}\bigl(\dots, m = 2,\, n = 1,\, r = 2\bigr). \] The hypothesis $r = 2 \leq \min(2, v_2(q - 1))$ requires $v_2(q-1) \geq 2$, equivalently $q \equiv 1 \pmod 4$.
nodes.label: def:canonicalC4OnCq-r2

nodes.name: $\varphi : C_2 \times C_2 \to \mathrm{Aut}(C_q)$, image of order $2$
nodes.statement: For an odd prime $q$, define \[ \mathtt{canonicalC2C2OnCqAction} := \mathtt{sdpCanonicalAction}\bigl(\dots, m = 1,\, n = 1,\, r = 1\bigr) \circ \mathrm{fst}, \] where $\mathrm{fst} : C_2 \times C_2 \to C_2$ is projection on the first factor. The resulting semidirect product $C_q \rtimes (C_2 \times C_2)$ is isomorphic to the dihedral group $D_{2q}$.
nodes.label: def:canonicalC2C2OnCq

nodes.name: Order-$3$ automorphism of $C_2 \times C_2$
nodes.statement: Let $\sigma : C_2 \times C_2 \to C_2 \times C_2$ be the automorphism $(x, y) \mapsto (xy, x)$. Then $\sigma^3 = \mathrm{id}$ and $\sigma$ has order exactly $3$ in $\mathrm{MulAut}(C_2 \times C_2)$.
nodes.label: def:c2c2OrderThreeAut

nodes.statement: $\mathrm{ord}(\sigma) = 3$.
nodes.label: lem:orderOf-c2c2OrderThreeAut

nodes.statement: Verify $\sigma^3 = \mathrm{id}$ by direct computation in $C_2 \times C_2$ using that every element has order dividing $2$, then exhibit a witness $(g, 1)$ with $g$ a generator of $C_2$ where $\sigma(g, 1) = (g, g) \neq (g, 1)$ to show $\sigma \neq \mathrm{id}$.

nodes.name: $\psi : C_3 \to \mathrm{Aut}(C_2 \times C_2)$ sending generator to $\sigma$
nodes.statement: Define $\mathtt{canonicalC3OnC2C2Action} : C_3 \to \mathrm{MulAut}(C_2 \times C_2)$ by extending the assignment (generator of $C_3$) $\mapsto \sigma$ to a group homomorphism, which is well-defined because $|\sigma| = 3 = |C_3|$.
nodes.label: def:canonicalC3OnC2C2

nodes.name: Range cardinality of $\psi$
nodes.statement: The image of $\mathtt{canonicalC3OnC2C2Action}$ has cardinality $3$.
nodes.label: lem:canonicalC3OnC2C2-range

nodes.statement: The range equals $\langle \sigma \rangle$, whose cardinality is $\mathrm{ord}(\sigma) = 3$.

nodes.name: Uniqueness of semidirect product $C_3 \to \mathrm{Aut}(C_2 \times C_2)$ with image of order $3$
nodes.statement: Let $f_1, f_2 : C_3 \to \mathrm{Aut}(C_2 \times C_2)$ both have image of cardinality $3$. Then $(C_2 \times C_2) \rtimes_{f_1} C_3 \cong (C_2 \times C_2) \rtimes_{f_2} C_3$.
nodes.label: lem:sdp-C3-on-C2C2-iso

nodes.statement: $\mathrm{MulAut}(C_2 \times C_2) \cong D_3$ has a unique Sylow $3$-subgroup (since $|D_3| = 6 = 3 \cdot 2$ and $n_3 \equiv 1 \pmod 3$ with $n_3 \mid 2$ forces $n_3 = 1$). Hence both images coincide with this Sylow $3$-subgroup. Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:sdp-iso-range-eq} with $p = 3$.

nodes.name: Classification of groups of order $4q$ for $q \geq 3$ prime
nodes.statement: Let $q$ be a prime with $q \geq 3$ and let $G$ be a group with $|G| = 4q$. Then exactly one of the following holds: \begin{enumerate} \item $G \cong C_{4q}$. \item $G \cong C_2 \times C_2 \times C_q$. \item $G \cong C_q \rtimes_{\varphi_1} C_4$, where $\varphi_1$ is $\mathtt{canonicalC4OnCqAction}$ (image of order $2$). \item $q \equiv 1 \pmod 4$ and $G \cong C_q \rtimes_{\varphi_2} C_4$, where $\varphi_2$ is $\mathtt{canonicalC4OnCqAction\_r2}$ (image of order $4$). \item $G \cong C_q \rtimes_\varphi (C_2 \times C_2)$, where $\varphi$ is $\mathtt{canonicalC2C2OnCqAction}$ (image of order $2$); this group is isomorphic to $D_{2q}$. \item $q = 3$ and $G \cong (C_2 \times C_2) \rtimes_\psi C_3$, where $\psi$ is $\mathtt{canonicalC3OnC2C2Action}$; this group is isomorphic to $A_4$. \end{enumerate} Implemented as \texttt{classification\_4q} in \texttt{M2rGroup7.P2qClassification.FourQClassification}.
nodes.label: thm:classification-4q

nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:p2q-normal-sylow} applied with $p = 2$, either the Sylow $2$-subgroup or the Sylow $q$-subgroup of $G$ is normal. \emph{Case 1: normal Sylow $2$-subgroup $P$.} By Lemma~\ref{lem:sylow-card-index}, $|P| = 4$ and $[G:P] = q$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:schur-zassenhaus} (with $\gcd(4, q) = 1$) there is a complement $K \leq G$ with $|K| = q$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:sdp-from-complement}, $G \cong P \rtimes_\varphi K$ for some $\varphi$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:prime-classification}, $K \cong C_q$. \begin{itemize} \item If $P \cong C_4$: by Lemma~\ref{lem:aut-cyclic-p2}, $\mathrm{Aut}(P) \cong C_2$. Since $\gcd(q, 2) = 1$, by Lemma~\ref{lem:eq-one-of-coprime-card}, $\varphi = 1$. Combine Lemma~\ref{lem:sdp-trivial-action} and Lemma~\ref{lem:cyclic-prod} to get $G \cong C_{4q}$ (outcome 1). \item If $P \cong C_2 \times C_2$: by Lemma~\ref{lem:aut-CpCp} and Lemma~\ref{lem:GL2F2-isoS3}, $|\mathrm{Aut}(P)| = 6$. If $q > 3$, then $\gcd(q, 6) = 1$ and Lemma~\ref{lem:eq-one-of-coprime-card} forces $\varphi = 1$, giving $G \cong C_2 \times C_2 \times C_q$ (outcome 2). If $q = 3$, we split on whether $\varphi$ is trivial. If yes, $G \cong C_2 \times C_2 \times C_3$ (outcome 2). If no, transport $\varphi$ along $P \cong C_2 \times C_2$ and $K \cong C_3$ to a nontrivial $\varphi' : C_3 \to \mathrm{Aut}(C_2 \times C_2)$. Its image has cardinality $3$ (since the image is a non-trivial subgroup of the cyclic $C_3$). By Lemma~\ref{lem:canonicalC3OnC2C2-range} and Lemma~\ref{lem:sdp-C3-on-C2C2-iso}, $G$ is isomorphic to the semidirect product with $\mathtt{canonicalC3OnC2C2Action}$ (outcome 6). \end{itemize} \emph{Case 2: normal Sylow $q$-subgroup $Q$.} By Lemma~\ref{lem:sylow-card-index}, $|Q| = q$ and $[G:Q] = 4$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:schur-zassenhaus} there is a complement $K$ with $|K| = 4$, and by Lemma~\ref{lem:sdp-from-complement}, $G \cong Q \rtimes_\varphi K$ with $\varphi : K \to \mathrm{Aut}(Q)$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:prime-classification}, $Q \cong C_q$. \begin{itemize} \item If $K \cong C_4$: transport $\varphi$ across $Q \cong C_q$ and $K \cong C_4$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:sdp-congr}) to obtain $\varphi' : C_4 \to \mathrm{Aut}(C_q)$. Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:classify-sdp} with $p = 2$, $m = 2$, $n = 1$ to get a unique $r \in \{0, 1, 2\} \cap \{0, \dots, \min(2, v_2(q-1))\}$ and an isomorphism to the canonical $\psi_r$-semidirect product. \begin{itemize} \item $r = 0$: $\psi_0$ has image of cardinality $1$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:sdp-canonical-range}, so $\psi_0 = 1$; Lemma~\ref{lem:sdp-trivial-action} and Lemma~\ref{lem:cyclic-prod} give $G \cong C_q \times C_4 \cong C_{4q}$ (outcome 1). \item $r = 1$: $\psi_1$ equals $\mathtt{canonicalC4OnCqAction}$ by definitional equality (same head function, same explicit arguments, proof arguments equal by proof irrelevance), giving outcome 3. \item $r = 2$: forces $\min(2, v_2(q-1)) \geq 2$ hence $v_2(q-1) \geq 2$ hence $q \equiv 1 \pmod 4$; $\psi_2$ equals $\mathtt{canonicalC4OnCqAction\_r2}$ by definitional equality, giving outcome 4. \end{itemize} \item If $K \cong C_2 \times C_2$: if $\varphi = 1$ then Lemma~\ref{lem:sdp-trivial-action} gives $G \cong C_q \times C_2 \times C_2 \cong C_2 \times C_2 \times C_q$ (outcome 2). Otherwise, transport $\varphi$ to $\varphi' : C_2 \times C_2 \to \mathrm{Aut}(C_q)$; its image is a subgroup of $\mathrm{Aut}(C_q) \cong C_{q-1}$ and thus cyclic. The image cardinality divides $|C_2 \times C_2| = 4$ and divides $|\mathrm{Aut}(C_q)| = q - 1$, but also (as a hom from $C_2 \times C_2$ into a cyclic group) divides $2$; combined with $\varphi' \neq 1$, the image has cardinality exactly $2$. $\mathtt{canonicalC2C2OnCqAction}$ has the same image cardinality (Definition~\ref{def:canonicalC2C2OnCq}), so by \texttt{semidirectProduct\_CpCp\_iso} (a $C_p \times C_p$ analogue of Lemma~\ref{lem:sdp-iso-range-eq}; see \texttt{M2rGroup7.Lemmas.ClassificationUtils}) the two semidirect products are isomorphic, giving outcome 5. \end{itemize}

The complete classification of groups of order $4q$ for $q \equiv 3 \pmod 4$ contains four isomorphism types, the two above together with $C_q \rtimes C_4$ (nontrivial) and $C_q \rtimes (C_2 \times C_2) \cong D_{2q}$. The current target theorem in this blueprint asserts only the disjunction $G \cong C_{4q}$ or $G \cong C_2 \times C_2 \times C_q$; the nontrivial semidirect-product cases (Case 2 of the proof) are documented here but treated as a residual TODO.

nodes.name: A group of order $p^2 q$ has a normal Sylow subgroup
nodes.statement: Let $p, q$ be distinct primes and let $G$ be a finite group of order $p^2 q$. Then either the number of Sylow $p$-subgroups of $G$ is $1$ (so the unique Sylow $p$-subgroup is normal) or the number of Sylow $q$-subgroups of $G$ is $1$ (so the unique Sylow $q$-subgroup is normal).
nodes.label: lem:p2q-normal-sylow

nodes.statement: Standard Sylow counting. Already established in the repository as \texttt{p2q\_group\_has\_normal\_sylow\_subgroup}.

nodes.name: Sylow cardinality and index
nodes.statement: Let $p, q$ be distinct primes, $a, b \in \mathbb{N}$, and let $G$ be a finite group with $|G| = p^a q^b$. Then every Sylow $p$-subgroup of $G$ has order $p^a$ and index $q^b$.
nodes.label: lem:sylow-card-index

nodes.statement: From $|G| = p^a q^b$ and coprimality of $p^a$ and $q^b$, the multiplicity of $p$ in $|G|$ is $a$, so every Sylow $p$-subgroup has order $p^a$ by Mathlib's \texttt{Sylow.card\_eq\_multiplicity}. The index is then $|G|/p^a = q^b$ by Lagrange. Already established as \texttt{sylow\_card\_eq} and \texttt{sylow\_index\_eq}.

nodes.name: Cyclic classification of prime order
nodes.statement: If $|G| = n$ with $n$ prime, then $G \cong C_n$.
nodes.label: lem:prime-classification

nodes.statement: A group of prime order has a generator (any non-identity element), hence is cyclic. Two cyclic groups of equal finite order are isomorphic via Mathlib's \texttt{mulEquivOfCyclicCardEq}. Already established as \texttt{prime\_classification}.

nodes.name: Classification of groups of order $p^2$
nodes.statement: For any prime $p$, a group of order $p^2$ is isomorphic to either $C_{p^2}$ or $C_p \times C_p$.
nodes.label: lem:p-squared-classification

nodes.statement: Any group of order $p^2$ is abelian; either it is cyclic (and isomorphic to $C_{p^2}$) or it has exponent $p$, in which case it is a $2$-dimensional $\mathbb{F}_p$-vector space. Already established as \texttt{p\_squared\_classification}.

nodes.name: Aut$(C_{p^2}) \cong C_{p(p-1)}$
nodes.statement: For any prime $p$, $\mathrm{MulAut}(C_{p^2}) \cong C_{p(p-1)}$.
nodes.label: lem:aut-cyclic-p2

nodes.statement: $\mathrm{MulAut}(C_{p^2}) \cong (\mathbb{Z}/p^2 \mathbb{Z})^\times$, which is cyclic of order $\varphi(p^2) = p(p-1)$. Already established as \texttt{aut\_of\_cyclic\_p2}.

nodes.name: Aut$(C_p \times C_p) \cong \mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{F}_p)$
nodes.statement: For any prime $p$, $\mathrm{MulAut}(C_p \times C_p) \cong \mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{F}_p)$.
nodes.label: lem:aut-CpCp

nodes.statement: $C_p \times C_p$ is a $2$-dimensional $\mathbb{F}_p$-vector space and every additive automorphism is automatically $\mathbb{F}_p$-linear. Already established as \texttt{aut\_of\_CpCp}.

nodes.name: $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{F}_2) \cong S_3$
nodes.statement: $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{F}_2)$ is isomorphic to the dihedral group of order $6$ (equivalently, $S_3$).
nodes.label: lem:GL2F2-isoS3

nodes.statement: A computation: $|\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{F}_2)| = 6$ and $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{F}_2)$ is non-abelian, so by the classification of groups of order $6$ it must be isomorphic to $D_3$. Already established as \texttt{GL2F2\_isoS3}.

nodes.name: Trivial homomorphism from coprime cardinalities
nodes.statement: Let $G, H$ be finite groups with $\gcd(|G|, |H|) = 1$. Then every group homomorphism $\varphi : G \to H$ is the trivial homomorphism $\varphi = 1$.
nodes.label: lem:eq-one-of-coprime-card

nodes.statement: The image $\varphi(G)$ is a subgroup of $H$ whose order divides both $|G|$ and $|H|$, hence divides $\gcd(|G|,|H|) = 1$. Therefore $|\varphi(G)| = 1$, so $\varphi(G) = \{1\}$, so $\varphi = 1$. Already established as \texttt{eq\_one\_of\_coprime\_card}.

nodes.name: Semidirect product with trivial action is a direct product
nodes.statement: Let $N, K$ be groups and let $\varphi : K \to \mathrm{Aut}(N)$ be a homomorphism with $\varphi = 1$. Then $N \rtimes_\varphi K \cong N \times K$.
nodes.label: lem:sdp-trivial-action

nodes.statement: The underlying set of $N \rtimes_\varphi K$ is $N \times K$ and the multiplication $(n_1, k_1)(n_2, k_2) = (n_1 \cdot \varphi(k_1)(n_2),\ k_1 k_2)$ reduces to $(n_1 n_2, k_1 k_2)$ when $\varphi \equiv 1$. Hence the identity pair map is a group isomorphism. Already established as \texttt{SemidirectProduct.mulEquivOfTrivialAction}.

nodes.name: Coprime cyclic direct product
nodes.statement: For positive integers $m, n$ with $\gcd(m, n) = 1$, $C_m \times C_n \cong C_{mn}$.
nodes.label: lem:cyclic-prod

nodes.statement: $C_m \times C_n$ is cyclic (the direct product of two cyclic groups of coprime orders is cyclic, since one can take the product of generators and apply the Chinese Remainder Theorem on orders), and has cardinality $mn$. Already established as \texttt{CyclicGroup.prodMulEquiv}.

nodes.name: Schur--Zassenhaus complement
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be a finite group and $N \trianglelefteq G$ a normal subgroup such that $\gcd(|N|, [G : N]) = 1$. Then there exists a subgroup $K \leq G$ with $N \cap K = \{1\}$ and $N K = G$ (a right complement to $N$ in $G$).
nodes.label: lem:schur-zassenhaus

nodes.statement: The Schur--Zassenhaus theorem, available in Mathlib as \texttt{Subgroup.exists\_right\_complement'\_of\_coprime}.

nodes.name: Semidirect product from a complement
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be a group, $N \trianglelefteq G$ a normal subgroup, and $K \leq G$ a complement of $N$ (so $N \cap K = \{1\}$ and $NK = G$). Then $G \cong N \rtimes_\varphi K$, where $\varphi : K \to \mathrm{Aut}(N)$ is the conjugation action.
nodes.label: lem:sdp-from-complement

nodes.statement: Mathlib provides this isomorphism as \texttt{SemidirectProduct.mulEquivSubgroup}.

nodes.name: Partial classification of groups of order $4q$
nodes.statement: Let $q$ be a prime with $q > 3$ and $q \equiv 3 \pmod 4$, and let $G$ be a group with $|G| = 4q$. Then \[ G \cong C_{4q} \quad \text{or} \quad G \cong C_2 \times C_2 \times C_q. \] (This is a partial classification: when the unique Sylow $q$-subgroup is normal and the conjugation action is nontrivial, $G$ falls outside this disjunction; see the Case 2 discussion below for the residual cases.)
nodes.label: thm:classification-4q

nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:p2q-normal-sylow} applied with $p = 2$, either the Sylow $2$-subgroup or the Sylow $q$-subgroup of $G$ is normal. \emph{Case 1: Normal Sylow $2$-subgroup $P$ with $|P| = 4$ and $[G:P] = q$.} By Lemma~\ref{lem:sylow-card-index} we have $|P| = 4$ and $[G:P] = q$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:schur-zassenhaus} (with $\gcd(4, q) = 1$ since $q$ is an odd prime) there is a complement $K \leq G$ with $|K| = q$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:sdp-from-complement}, $G \cong P \rtimes_\varphi K$ for some $\varphi : K \to \mathrm{Aut}(P)$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:prime-classification}, $K \cong C_q$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:p-squared-classification}, $P \cong C_4$ or $P \cong C_2 \times C_2$. Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:case1-c4} or Lemma~\ref{lem:case1-c2c2} accordingly to conclude $G \cong C_{4q}$ or $G \cong C_2 \times C_2 \times C_q$. \emph{Case 2: Normal Sylow $q$-subgroup $N$ with $|N| = q$ and $[G:N] = 4$.} By Lemma~\ref{lem:sylow-card-index}, $|N| = q$ and $[G:N] = 4$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:schur-zassenhaus} there is a complement $K$ with $|K| = 4$ and by Lemma~\ref{lem:sdp-from-complement}, $G \cong N \rtimes_\varphi K$ with $N \cong C_q$ and $K \cong C_4$ or $C_2 \times C_2$. When $\varphi$ is trivial, $G \cong C_q \times K$, which gives $G \cong C_{4q}$ (if $K \cong C_4$, by Lemma~\ref{lem:cyclic-prod}) or $G \cong C_2 \times C_2 \times C_q$ (if $K \cong C_2 \times C_2$). When $\varphi$ is nontrivial, the resulting semidirect product is not isomorphic to either group in the disjunction; these subcases lie outside the current target theorem and are listed as TODO in the discussion of Case 2 below.

nodes.name: Case 1.1: $P \cong C_4$ gives $G \cong C_{4q}$
nodes.statement: Let $q$ be an odd prime, let $P$ be a group with $P \cong C_4$, let $K$ be a group with $K \cong C_q$, and let $\varphi : K \to \mathrm{MulAut}(P)$ be any homomorphism. Then $P \rtimes_\varphi K \cong C_{4q}$.
nodes.label: lem:case1-c4

nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:aut-cyclic-p2} applied to $p = 2$ and using $P \cong C_4 = C_{2^2}$, we have $\mathrm{MulAut}(P) \cong C_{2 \cdot 1} = C_2$, so $|\mathrm{MulAut}(P)| = 2$. Since $q > 2$ is an odd prime, $\gcd(q, 2) = 1$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:eq-one-of-coprime-card} applied to $\varphi : K \to \mathrm{MulAut}(P)$, $\varphi$ is trivial. By Lemma~\ref{lem:sdp-trivial-action}, $P \rtimes_\varphi K \cong P \times K \cong C_4 \times C_q$. Finally, by Lemma~\ref{lem:cyclic-prod} with $\gcd(4, q) = 1$, we conclude $C_4 \times C_q \cong C_{4q}$.

nodes.name: Case 1.2: $P \cong C_2 \times C_2$ gives $G \cong C_2 \times C_2 \times C_q$
nodes.statement: Let $q$ be a prime with $q > 3$, let $P$ be a group with $P \cong C_2 \times C_2$, let $K$ be a group with $K \cong C_q$, and let $\varphi : K \to \mathrm{MulAut}(P)$ be any homomorphism. Then $P \rtimes_\varphi K \cong C_2 \times C_2 \times C_q$.
nodes.label: lem:case1-c2c2

nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:aut-CpCp}, $\mathrm{MulAut}(C_2 \times C_2) \cong \mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{F}_2)$, and by Lemma~\ref{lem:GL2F2-isoS3}, $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{F}_2) \cong D_3$ (a group of order $6$). Hence $|\mathrm{MulAut}(P)| = 6 = 2 \cdot 3$. Since $q$ is prime with $q > 3$, $q$ is coprime to both $2$ and $3$, hence $\gcd(q, 6) = 1$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:eq-one-of-coprime-card}, $\varphi : K \to \mathrm{MulAut}(P)$ is trivial. By Lemma~\ref{lem:sdp-trivial-action}, $P \rtimes_\varphi K \cong P \times K \cong (C_2 \times C_2) \times C_q \cong C_2 \times C_2 \times C_q$ (the last step is reassociation of the direct product, an instance of \texttt{MulEquiv.prodAssoc}).
\leanfile{M2rGroup7/Lemmas/LinearAlgebraUtils.lean} The element $\operatorname{diag}(1, -1) \in \mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{F}_p)$.
nodes.label: def:gl2-diag-one-neg-one

nodes.statement: \leanfile{M2rGroup7/Lemmas/LinearAlgebraUtils.lean} The element $\operatorname{diag}(-1, -1) = -I \in \mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{F}_p)$.
nodes.label: def:gl2-diag-neg-one-neg-one

nodes.statement: \leanfile{M2rGroup7/Lemmas/LinearAlgebraUtils.lean} Let $p$ be an odd prime and let $A \in \mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{F}_p)$ be an element of order $2$. Then $A$ is conjugate in $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{F}_p)$ to either $\operatorname{diag}(1, -1)$ or to $\operatorname{diag}(-1, -1) = -I$.
nodes.label: thm:gl2-order-two-classification

nodes.statement:
Let $M = A$ regarded as a matrix. Since $A$ has order $2$, we have $M^2 = I$ and $M 
eq I$. If $M = -I$, then $A = \operatorname{diag}(-1, -1)$ is conjugate to itself by the identity, giving the second alternative. Otherwise $M 
eq I$ and $M 
eq -I$. Since $M^2 - I = (M - I)(M + I) = 0$ and $M 
eq -I$, the matrix $M + I$ is nonzero, so it has a nonzero column $v_+$. From $(M - I)(M + I) = 0$ we get $M v_+ = v_+$, i.e.\ $v_+$ is a $1$-eigenvector. Similarly, since $M 
eq I$, the matrix $M - I$ is nonzero, so it has a nonzero column $v_-$, and $(M + I)(M - I) = 0$ gives $M v_- = -v_-$, so $v_-$ is a $(-1)$-eigenvector. Because $1 
eq -1$ in $\mathbb{F}_p$ (this is where we use $p 
eq 2$), eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues are linearly independent, so $\{v_+, v_-\}$ is a basis of $\mathbb{F}_p^2$. The change-of-basis matrix $P = [\,v_+ \mid v_-\,]$ lies in $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{F}_p)$ and satisfies $M P = P \cdot \operatorname{diag}(1, -1)$, i.e.\ $P^{-1} M P = \operatorname{diag}(1, -1)$. Hence $A$ is conjugate to $\operatorname{diag}(1, -1)$, giving the first alternative.

\leanfile{M2rGroup7/Lemmas/GroupTheoryLemmas.lean} The \emph{fixed-point subgroup} $\operatorname{Fix}(\operatorname{Im} f)\le N$ of $f$ is \[ \operatorname{Fix}(\operatorname{Im} f) \;=\; \{\, n \in N \;:\; f(h)(n) = n \text{ for every } h \in K \,\}. \] It is a subgroup because $f(h)$ is a group automorphism of $N$ for every $h \in K$.
nodes.section: 23 Centre of a semidirect product of abelian groups
nodes.label: def:fixedPointsSubgroup

nodes.statement: \leanfile{M2rGroup7/Lemmas/GroupTheoryLemmas.lean} Let $N, K$ be abelian groups and $f : K \to \operatorname{Aut}(N)$. For $g = (n, h) \in N\rtimes_f K$, we have $g \in Z(N\rtimes_f K)$ if and only if \[ h \in \ker f \qquad\text{and}\qquad f(h')(n) = n \text{ for every } h' \in K. \]
nodes.section: 23 Centre of a semidirect product of abelian groups
nodes.label: lem:mem_center_semidirectProduct_iff

nodes.statement: Write $g = (n, h)$ and let $x = (x', y') \in N\rtimes_f K$ be arbitrary. By definition of the operation, the commutativity relation $g x = x g$ reads \[ \bigl(n\cdot f(h)(x'),\, h y'\bigr) \;=\; \bigl(x'\cdot f(y')(n),\, y' h\bigr). \] Because $K$ is abelian, the right components automatically agree. Hence $g\in Z(N\rtimes_f K)$ is equivalent to \[ n\cdot f(h)(x') \;=\; x' \cdot f(y')(n) \qquad \text{for all } x' \in N,\ y' \in K. \tag{$\ast$} \] Setting $y' = 1$ in $(\ast)$ gives $n\cdot f(h)(x') = x' \cdot n$, and since $N$ is abelian we may cancel to get $f(h)(x') = x'$ for every $x' \in N$, i.e.\ $f(h) = \mathrm{id}$, i.e.\ $h \in \ker f$. Setting $x' = 1$ in $(\ast)$ and using $h \in \ker f$ gives $n = f(y')(n)$ for every $y' \in K$, i.e.\ $n \in \operatorname{Fix}(\operatorname{Im} f)$. Conversely, if both conditions hold then $f(h) = \mathrm{id}$ and $f(y')(n) = n$, so \[ (n, h)(x', y') = (n\cdot x',\, h y') = (x'\cdot n,\, y' h) = (x', y')(n, h), \] using that $N$ and $K$ are abelian.
nodes.section: 23 Centre of a semidirect product of abelian groups

nodes.statement: \leanfile{M2rGroup7/Lemmas/GroupTheoryLemmas.lean} Let $N, K$ be abelian groups and $f : K \to \operatorname{Aut}(N)$. There is a group isomorphism \[ Z(N\rtimes_f K) \;\simeq\; \operatorname{Fix}(\operatorname{Im} f) \times \ker f \] sending the class of $(n, h) \in Z(N\rtimes_f K)$ to $(n, h)$.
nodes.section: 23 Centre of a semidirect product of abelian groups
nodes.label: lem:center_semidirectProduct_iso

nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:mem_center_semidirectProduct_iff}, the map \[ (n, h) \in Z(N\rtimes_f K) \;\longmapsto\; (n, h) \in \operatorname{Fix}(\operatorname{Im} f) \times \ker f \] is well defined. It is a homomorphism: for $g_1 = (n_1, h_1)$ and $g_2 = (n_2, h_2)$ both in the centre, $h_1 \in \ker f$ implies $f(h_1) = \mathrm{id}$, so \[ g_1 g_2 = (n_1 \cdot f(h_1)(n_2),\, h_1 h_2) = (n_1 n_2,\, h_1 h_2), \] which matches the componentwise product. Injectivity is immediate, and surjectivity is the converse direction of Lemma~\ref{lem:mem_center_semidirectProduct_iff}.
nodes.section: 23 Centre of a semidirect product of abelian groups

nodes.statement: Let $f : K \rightarrow \text{Aut}(N)$ be the underlying homomorphism of $N \rtimes K$ where $N, K$ are abelian groups. Then $Z(N \rtimes K) = \text{Fix}(\text{Im}(f)) \times \text{Ker}(f)$
nodes.section: 23 Centre of a semidirect product of abelian groups
nodes.label: Centre of semidirect product

nodes.statement: Group operation is defined as $$(x_1, y_1)(x_2, y_2) = (x_1 \cdot f(y_1)(x_2), y_1y_2)$$ By definition $(x, y) \in Z(G) \iff$ for arbitrary $(x', y') \in G$ we have: $$(x, y)(x', y') = (x', y')(x, y)$$ Using the definition of the group operation, this is equivalent to $$(x \cdot f(y)(x'), yy') = (x' \cdot f(y')(x), y'y)$$ Since $K$ is abelian, we always have $yy' = y'y$. Thus the condition simplifies to $$(x, y) \in Z(G) \iff x \cdot f(y)(x') = x' \cdot f(y')(x) \text{ } \forall x' \in N, y' \in K$$ Setting $y' = 1$ we get $x \cdot f(y)(x') = x' \cdot x \implies f(y)(x') = x'$ (as $N$ is abelian) which shows that $y \in \text{Ker}(f)$ as $x'$ is arbitrary. Setting $x' = 1$ we get $x = f(y')(x)$ (using $y \in \text{Ker}(f)$). Hence $x \in \text{Fix}(\text{Im}(f))$ as $y'$ is arbitrary. These conditions are necessary and sufficient as one can show that $(x, y)(x', y') = (x \cdot x', y \cdot y') = (x' \cdot x, y' \cdot y) = (x', y') (x, y)$.
nodes.section: 23 Centre of a semidirect product of abelian groups

nodes.statement: Let $G$ be a finite group of order $pqr$ for distinct primes $p < q < r$. Then either the Sylow-$q$ subgroup or the Sylow-$r$ subgroup of $G$ is normal, i.e.\ $n_q(G) = 1$ or $n_r(G) = 1$.
nodes.label: pqr_normal_sylow

nodes.statement: By Sylow's theorems $n_r \equiv 1 \pmod r$ and $n_r \mid pq$, so $n_r \in \{1, p, q, pq\}$. Neither $p$ nor $q$ is congruent to $1$ modulo $r$ because both are smaller than $r$ and at least $2$. If $n_r = 1$ we are done, so assume $n_r = pq$. Distinct Sylow-$r$ subgroups have prime order $r$, so they intersect trivially; the total number of elements of order $r$ is therefore $pq(r-1)$. Now $n_q \mid pr$ and $n_q \equiv 1 \pmod q$. Suppose for contradiction $n_q > 1$. Then $n_q \geq q + 1$, so $n_q \in \{r, pr\}$ (since $p < q$, $n_q = p$ is impossible). In either case $n_q \geq r$, giving at least $r(q-1) \geq q+r-1$ elements of order $q$. Adding the elements of order $r$ and the identity: \[ 1 + pq(r-1) + r(q-1) = 1 + pqr - pq + qr - r > pqr, \] since $qr > pq + r - 1$ follows from $r > p$ and $q \geq 3$. Contradiction.
Let $G$ be a finite group of order $pqr$ for distinct primes $p < q < r$. Then $G$ has a normal subgroup of order $qr$.
nodes.label: pqr_normal_subgroup_qr

nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{pqr_normal_sylow} either $n_q = 1$ or $n_r = 1$. Pick a Sylow-$q$ subgroup $Q$ and a Sylow-$r$ subgroup $R$. The two subgroups have coprime orders, so $Q \cap R = \{1\}$ and hence $|QR| = |Q|\,|R| = qr$. If $Q$ is normal then $QR$ is a subgroup (as $Q \lhd G$), of order $qr$ and index $p$. Since $p$ is the smallest prime dividing $|G|$, the subgroup $QR$ is normal. The case where $R$ is normal is symmetric.
Let $G$ be a group with $|G| = 30$. Then $G$ is isomorphic to exactly one of $C_{30}$, $D_{15}$, $C_5 \times D_3$, $C_3 \times D_5$.
nodes.label: order_30_classification

nodes.statement: By Theorem~\ref{pqr_normal_subgroup_qr} (with $p=2$, $q=3$, $r=5$), $G$ has a normal subgroup $N$ of order $15$. By Schur--Zassenhaus there is a complementary subgroup $U \leq G$ of order $2$ with $G \cong N \rtimes U$. We have $U \cong C_2$, and by the classification of groups of order $pq$ with $p \nmid q-1$ (taking $p=3$, $q=5$, where $3 \nmid 4$) we have $N \cong C_{15}$. Let $\phi : C_2 \to \mathrm{Aut}(C_{15})$ be the underlying homomorphism. The image $\mathrm{Im}\,\phi$ has order $1$ or $2$. \paragraph{Case 1: $|\mathrm{Im}\,\phi| = 1$.} The action is trivial, so $G \cong C_{15} \times C_2 \cong C_{30}$. \paragraph{Case 2: $|\mathrm{Im}\,\phi| = 2$.} We have $\mathrm{Aut}(C_{15}) \cong (\mathbb{Z}/15\mathbb{Z})^\times \cong (\mathbb{Z}/3)^\times \times (\mathbb{Z}/5)^\times \cong C_2 \times C_4$, which has exactly three elements of order two: those acting by \begin{itemize} \item inverting both factors (the global inversion automorphism of $C_{15}$), \item inverting only the $C_3$ factor, \item inverting only the $C_5$ factor. \end{itemize} By Lemma~\ref{equal_image_iso_sdp} (\textit{equal images give isomorphic semi-direct products for cyclic $p$-groups in the acting position}), each choice gives one isomorphism class. The three resulting groups, written in their direct product form, are: \begin{itemize} \item $\phi$ inverts both $C_3$ and $C_5$: $G \cong D_{15}$. \item $\phi$ inverts only $C_3$ and fixes $C_5$: $G \cong (C_3 \rtimes_{\mathrm{inv}} C_2) \times C_5 \cong D_3 \times C_5$. \item $\phi$ fixes $C_3$ and inverts $C_5$: $G \cong C_3 \times (C_5 \rtimes_{\mathrm{inv}} C_2) \cong C_3 \times D_5$. \end{itemize} Combined with Case~1, we obtain the four isomorphism classes claimed.
If $K$ is a cyclic $p$-group, two homomorphisms $f, g : K \to \mathrm{Aut}(H)$ with the same image define isomorphic semi-direct products $H \rtimes_f K$ and $H \rtimes_g K$.
nodes.label: equal_image_iso_sdp

nodes.statement: Let $k$ be a generator of $K$. Since $\mathrm{Im}(f) = \langle f(k) \rangle = \langle g(k) \rangle$, there exists $n$ with $\gcd(n, |\mathrm{Im}(f)|) = 1$ such that $g(k) = f(k)^n$. As $\mathrm{Im}(f)$ has order $p^j$ for some $j \geq 0$, this $n$ is coprime to $|K| = p^m$. The map $\beta(x) = x^n$ is then an automorphism of $K$, and $g = f \circ \beta$. The pair $(\mathrm{id}_H, \beta)$ induces an isomorphism $H \rtimes_g K \cong H \rtimes_f K$.

nodes.name: First Sylow Theorem
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be a finite group and $p$ be a prime such that $p \mid |G|$. Then $G$ has a subgroup of order $p^{v_p(|G|)}$.

nodes.name: Second Sylow Theorem
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be a finite group and $p$ be a prime such that $p \mid |G|$. Then $n_p(G) \equiv 1 \pmod p$.

nodes.name: Fourth Sylow Theorem
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be a finite group and $p$ be a prime such that $p \mid |G|$. The Sylow-$p$ groups of $G$ form a single conjugacy class.
Let $G$ be a finite group and $p$ be a prime such that $p \mid |G|$. Then $n_p(G) \mid |G|$.
Let $G$ be a finite group. If $n_p(G) = 1$, then the unique Sylow-$p$ group of $G$ is normal.

nodes.name: Schur-zassenhaus
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be a finite group and let $N$ be a normal subgroup. Further suppose that $|N|$ and $|G/N|$ are co-prime. Then $G$ is isomorphic to some semi-direct product $N \rtimes G/N$.

nodes.name: With Claude
nodes.statement: All groups $G$ of order $p^2 q$ have either a normal Sylow-$p$ group or a normal Sylow $q$ group.
nodes.label: Groups of order $p^2 q$ have normal Sylow subgroup

nodes.statement: By Sylow's theorems, $n_p \mid q$, $n_p \equiv 1 \pmod p$, $n_q \mid p^2$, $n_q \equiv 1 \pmod q$. Hence $n_q$ is either $1, p$ or $p^2$ and $n_p$ is either $1$ or $q$. Case 1: $p < q$ If $n_q = p$ then $p \equiv 1 \pmod q$, contradicting $p < q$ as $p \neq 1$. If $n_q = p^2$ then we can perform a counting argument. We have $p^2$ Sylow-$q$ groups and they are trivially intersecting as they have prime order. Hence we get $p^2 (q - 1)$ elements of order $q$. As $n_p \geq 1$, the remaining $p^2$ elements must form a Sylow-$p$ group, hence $n_p = 1$, and so there is a normal Sylow-$p$ group. Otherwise $n_q = 1$ and so there exists a normal Sylow-$q$ group in that case. Case 2: $p > q$ If $n_p = q$, then we have a contradiction to $n_p \equiv 1 \pmod p$ as $q < p$ and $q \neq 1$. Hence $n_p = 1$ and there exists a normal Sylow-$p$ group.

nodes.name: With Gemini
nodes.statement: If $K$ is a cyclic $p$-group, two homomorphisms $f, g : K \rightarrow \text{Aut}(H)$ define isomorphic semi-direct products $H \rtimes K$ if they have the same image.
nodes.label: $K$ cyclic $p$-group then equal images define isomorphic semi-direct products

nodes.statement: It suffices to find an automorphism $\beta \in \text{Aut}(H)$ such that $g = f \circ \beta$. Let $k$ be a generator of $K$. We have that $\text{Im}(f) = \langle f(k) \rangle$ and $\text{Im}(g) = \langle g(k) \rangle$. As the images are equal, we get that $g(k) \in \langle f(k) \rangle$ and so there exists $n$ such that $g(k) = f(k)^n$ where $\gcd(n, |\text{Im}(f)|) = 1$. By the first isomorphism theorem, $\text{Im}(f) \cong K / \ker(f)$, hence $\text{Im}(f)$ has order $p^j$ for $0 \leq j \leq m$. If $j = 0$ then we get that the image of $f, g$ is the trivial group, hence both of them lead to direct products which are clearly isomorphic. Otherwise $j > 0$ and we get that $\gcd(n, p^j) = 1$ so $p \nmid n$. Hence $\gcd(n, |K|) = 1$. So we can define the automorphism $\beta : K \rightarrow K$ as $\beta(x) = x^n$. It is well defined as $(xy)^n = x^n y^n$ follows from the fact that $K$ is abelian. It is injective because $x^n = 1$ implies $x = 1$ as the order of $x$ would have to divide $n$ and $|K|$ (by Lagrange's theorem) but their gcd is $1$. Surjectivity then follows from the fact that it is injective and that it is a map from a finite group to itself. We have $g = f \circ \beta$ as they agree on a generator since $f(\beta(k)) = f(k^n) = f(k)^n = g(k)$.

nodes.name: With Gemini and Numina Fuse
nodes.statement: Semi-direct products $C_{q^n} \rtimes C_{p^m}$ ($q$ odd prime, $p \neq q$) are classified up to isomorphism by $r \in \{0, …, \min(m, d)\}$ where $d = v_p(q - 1)$, giving $\min(m, d) + 1$ classes. Every action $f$ belongs to exactly one class.
nodes.label: Classification of semi-direct products between Cyclic p-group and q-groups

nodes.statement: The fact that every action belongs to at least one class is a lot easier than showing that it belongs to exactly one class. We know that the semi direct product must have a homomorphism $f : C_{p^m} \rightarrow \text{Aut}(C_{q^n})$. We have $\text{Aut}(C_{q^n}) \cong C_{q^{n-1}(q - 1)}$. Thus, the image of $f$ (by first isomorphism theorem) can have order $p^r$ for some $0 \leq r \leq \min(v_p(q-1), m)$. Then we are done by the fact that a cyclic group has a unique subgroup given an order and that equal images imply isomorphic semi direct products (as $C_{p^m}$ is a cyclic $p$-group). For each $0 \leq r \leq \min(v_p(q-1), m)$ there does exist a homomorphism with image of order $p^r$. This can be constructed by sending the generator of $C_{p^m}$ to the element of $C_{q^{n-1}(q-1)}$ of order $p^r$. To show uniqueness, we will compute the orders of the centres given $r$. Claim 1: $Z(G) = \text{Fix}(\text{Im}(f)) \times \text{Ker}(f)$ Proof: Group operation is defined as $(x_1, y_1)(x_2, y_2) = (x_1 \cdot f(y_1)(x_2), y_1y_2)$. Thus $(x, y) \in Z(G) \iff$ for arbitrary $(x', y') \in G$ we have: $(x, y)(x', y') = (x', y')(x, y)$ or $(x \cdot f(y)(x'), yy') = (x' \cdot f(y')(x), y'y)$. As $C_{p^m}$ is abelian, we always have $yy' = y'y$. Thus $(x, y) \in Z(G) \iff x \cdot f(y)(x') = x' \cdot f(y')(x) \forall x' \in C_{q^n}, y' \in C_{p^m}$. Setting $y' = 1$ we get $x \cdot f(y)(x') = x' \cdot x \implies f(y)(x') = x'$ (as $C_{q^n}$ is abelian) which shows that $y \in \text{Ker}(f)$ as $x'$ is arbitrary. Setting $x' = 1$ we get $x = f(y')(x)$ (using $y \in \text{Ker}(f)$). Hence $x \in \text{Fix}(\text{Im}(f))$ as $y'$ is arbitrary. These conditions are necessary and sufficient as one can show that $(x, y)(x', y') = (x \cdot x', y \cdot y') = (x' \cdot x, y' \cdot y) = (x', y') (x, y)$. $\blacksquare$ If $r = 0$, the action is trivial, $\text{Im}(f) = \{\text{id}\}$ so every point gets fixed $\text{Fix}(\text{Im}(f)) = C_{q^n}$. Also $\text{Ker}(f) = C_{p^m}$ so $|Z(G)| = p^m q^n$. If $r > 0$, we have $|\text{Im}(f)| = p^r$. By the first Isomorphism theorem, $|\text{Ker}(f)| = \frac{|C_{p^m}|}{|\text{Im}(f)|} = p^{m - r}$. Claim 2: If $r > 0$, $|\text{Fix}(\text{Im}(f))| = 1$ Proof: A well known lemma (\mintinline{lean4}{IsPGroup.smul_mul_inv_trivial_or_surjective} in Mathlib) states that if a group $K$ acts on a cyclic $q$-group $G$ of coprime order, the map $\Psi : K \times G \to G$ defined by $(k, g) \mapsto k \bullet g \cdot g^{-1}$ is either trivial ($\Psi(k, g) = 1 \forall k, g \in K \times G$) or surjective. In our case, it is not surjective as that would mean $f$ has a trivial image but the image has order $p^r$ with $r > 0$. Hence $\Psi$ must be surjective. Let $x \in C_{q^n}$ be an arbitrary fixed point of the action. It suffices to show that $x = 1$. Using surjectivity of $\Psi$, there exists $k_0 \in C_{p^m}$ and $q_0 \in C_{q^n}$ satisfty $\Psi(k_0, q_0) = x \implies k_0 \bullet q_0 = x \cdot q_0$. One can inductively show that $k_0^s \bullet (k_0 \bullet q_0) = x^s \cdot (k_0 \bullet q_0)$ for any $s \geq 0$ (Sketch: $k_0 \bullet (k_0 \bullet q_0) = k_0 \bullet (x \cdot q_0) = (k_0 \bullet x) \cdot (k_0 \bullet q_0) = x \cdot (k_0 \bullet q_0)$). Substituting $s = p^m$ gives $k_0 \bullet q_0 = x^{p^m} \cdot (k_0 \bullet q_0)$ as $k_0$ has order $p^m$ because $k_0 \in C_{p^m}$. Hence $x^{p^m} = 1$. But $x \in C_{q^n}$ hence $x = 1$ as $p \neq q$. $\blacksquare$ Hence $|Z(G)| = p^{m - r}$. Clearly the order of all centres are distinct, which shows uniqueness.

nodes.name: Numina Fuse
nodes.statement: $s_2(p) = 2$ if $p$ is an odd prime.

We give both a short and elegant proof and a bashy one (by Numina Fuse) that is much simpler to formalise. Let $A \in GL_2(p)$ be of order $2$. Then its minimal polynomial divides $x^2 - 1$, hence it is a product of distinct linear factors ($1 
eq -1$ as $p$ is odd) and so is diagonalisable. The only matrix similar to identity is itself (and it doesn't have order $2$). Hence, $A$ must be similar to one of $	ext{diag}(-1, -1)$, $	ext{diag}(-1, 1)$ ($	ext{diag}(1, -1)$ is similar to $	ext{diag}(-1, 1)$) giving two similarity or conjugacy classes. eq I$. If $A = -I$, we are done. Otherwise, assume $A 
eq \pm I$. $A^2 = I$ implies: $a^2 + bc = 1$, $c(a + d) = 0$, $b(a + d) = 0$ and $bc + d^2 = 1$. If $c

nodes.name: Wild
nodes.statement: A quadruple $(N,\ n,\ \tau,\ v)$ is an \textit{extension type} if for group $N$, $v \in N$, $n \in \mathbb{N}^+$, $\tau \in \text{Aut}(N)$, $\tau (v) = v$ and $\tau^n = t_v$ (conjugate by $v$).

Although not explicitly defined in the text, a group $G$ is said to realise an extension type $(N,\ n,\ \tau,\ v)$ if: \begin{itemize} \item $N \lhd G$; \item There is an inducing element, $a \in G$, such that \item $\tau$ is exactly conjugating by $a$ for elements in $N$; \item $a^n = v$ (or, equivalently, the coset $Na$ has order $n$ in the quotient group $G/N$); \item The quotient group $G/N$ is isomorphic to a cyclic group of order $n$. \end{itemize}

nodes.name: Wild
nodes.statement: Two extension types, $(N,\ n,\ \tau,\ v)$ and $(N',\ n,\ \sigma,\ w)$ are said to be equivalent if there exists isomorphism $\phi : N \stackrel{\sim}{\smash{\rightarrow}\rule{0pt}{0.8ex}} N'$ such that $\sigma = \phi \circ \tau \circ \phi^{-1}$ and $w = \phi(v)$.

nodes.name: Wild
nodes.statement: Groups $G$ and $G'$ that realise equivalent extension types must be isomorphic.

nodes.name: Wild
nodes.statement: Take a group $N$. For some automorphic elements $v$ and $w$ in $N$ (i.e. there exists an automorphism which maps $v$ to $w$), and a fixed union of conjugacy classes from $\text{Aut}(N)$, $S$. Suppose for $\tau$ ranging over $S$ there is a group $G_\tau$ (and respectively $F_\tau$) which realises the extension type $(N,\ n,\ \tau,\ v)$ (and respectively $(N,\ n,\ \tau,\ w)$) for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$. Then the families $\{G_\tau | \tau \in S\}$ and $\{F_\tau | \tau \in S\}$ comprise the same isomorphism classes.

nodes.name: Wild
nodes.statement: Take a group $N$. For some characteristic element $v$ in $N$ (i.e. for any automorphism of $N$, $v$ is a fixed point). For any two groups $G$ and $G'$ such that they realise some extension types $(N,\ n,\ \tau,\ v)$ and $(N,\ n,\ \sigma,\ v)$ (respectively), if $\sigma$ and $\tau$ belongs to the same conjugacy class in $\text{Aut}(N)$, then $G$ and $G'$ are isomorphic.

nodes.statement: Lemma 3
A group $G$ of order $pqr$ for distinct primes $p < q < r$ must have either a normal Sylow-$r$ group or normal Sylow-$q$ group.
nodes.label: Groups of order $pqr$ have either a normal Sylow-$r$ group or normal Sylow-$q$ group

nodes.statement: By Sylow's theorems, we get $n_r \equiv 1 \pmod r$ and $n_r \mid pq$. If $n_r = 1$ we are done. $n_r = p$ or $q$ cannot hold because $p, q < r$ and $n_r \equiv 1 \pmod r$. Thus $n_r = pq$, and there are $pq(r-1)$ elements of order $r$. We have $n_q \mid pr, n_q \equiv 1 \pmod q$. Thus if $n_q > 1$, then $n_q \geq q + 1 > p + 1$. Hence, there are atleast $(p+1)(q-1) = pq + q - p - 1 \geq pq$ elements of order $q$, a contradiction as we already have $pqr$ elements but the identity has order $1$. Hence, $n_q = 1$ and we are done.
Let $N$ and $H$ be subgroups of $G$ with $N \lhd G$. Then $NH$ is a subgroup of $G$.

nodes.statement: Let $G$ be a finite group and $p$ be the smallest prime dividing $|G|$. Then any subgroup of $G$ of index $p$ is normal.
nodes.label: Subgroup of index smallest prime is normal

nodes.statement: A group $G$ of order $pqr$ for distinct primes $p < q < r$ has a normal subgroup of order $qr$
nodes.label: Group of order $pqr$ has a normal subgroup of order $qr$

nodes.statement: By \ref{Groups of order $pqr$ have either a normal Sylow-$r$ group or normal Sylow-$q$ group}, we either have a normal Sylow-$r$ group or normal Sylow-$q$ group. If we have a normal Sylow-$r$ group $N$, then $NH$ is a subgroup (by \ref{Product of subgroups is subgroup if one is normal}) of $G$ of order $qr$ (by \ref{Order of product of subgroups} and the fact that groups of prime order are trivially intersecting) where $H$ is any Sylow-$q$ group. Then $NH \lhd G$ follows from \ref{Subgroup of index smallest prime is normal}. An analogous argument holds for the case when there is a normal Sylow-$q$ group.
Let $G$ be a group of order $pq$ for primes $p < q$. Then $G$ has a normal Sylow-$q$ subgroup.

By Sylow's theorems, we get $n_q \equiv 1 \pmod q$ and $n_q \mid p$. If $n_q = p$, then as $p < q$, we we get a contradiction to $n_q \equiv 1 \pmod q$. Hence $n_q = 1$ and so $G$ has a normal Sylow-$q$ subgroup.
